title: AP Biology Study Guide 2026: All 8 Units & Exam Tips
summary: Use this AP Biology study guide to review all 8 units, key terms, FRQ verbs, exam weights, and high-impact study tips. Start preparing today.
body_markdown:
# AP Biology Study Guide 2026: All 8 Units & Exam Tips


**TL;DR:** This AP Biology study guide covers all 8 units, defines every essential term, and maps them to how they actually appear on the exam. Units 3, 6, and 7 account for up to 52% of your score, so they deserve the most study time. Students lose more points from misreading FRQ command verbs than from lacking biology knowledge, so this guide includes those definitions too. Bookmark this and come back to it throughout the year.


---


AP Biology is content-heavy. Eight units, hundreds of vocabulary terms, six science practices, and an exam that increasingly rewards application over memorization. A passing score is within reach (about 70% of test-takers scored a 3 or higher in 2025), but only if you study the right things in the right order.


This AP Biology study guide is organized as a working reference. Every term is grouped by unit, weighted by exam importance, and flagged for FRQ relevance. The goal is to give you something you can return to during every study session, not just read once and forget.


Before you start reviewing content, consider figuring out where your gaps are. A[diagnostic test](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/diagnostic-test) can help identify which units need the most attention, so you spend time where it counts.


## AP Biology Exam Format: Quick Reference


The AP Biology exam is 3 hours long and split evenly between two sections:


Section Format Time Weight


Section I 60 multiple-choice questions 90 minutes 50%


Section II 6 free-response questions 90 minutes 50%


The FRQ section breaks down into two long questions (9 points each) and four short questions (4 points each). Starting in 2026, the exam uses a hybrid digital format: you’ll answer multiple-choice questions and view FRQ prompts in Bluebook, then handwrite your free-response answers in a paper booklet.


### Unit Weight Distribution


This table should shape your entire study plan. Not all units are created equal.


Unit Topic Exam Weight


1 Chemistry of Life 8–11%


2 Cell Structure and Function 10–13%


3 **Cellular Energetics** **12–16%**


4 Cell Communication and Cell Cycle 10–15%


5 Heredity 8–11%


6 **Gene Expression and Regulation** **12–16%**


7 **Natural Selection** **13–20%**


8 Ecology 10–15%


Units 3, 6, and 7 combined account for 37–52% of the exam. If you’re short on time, these are where to focus. Unit 7 (Natural Selection) carries the single largest weight and shows up heavily in FRQs.


### Score Distribution Context


In 2025, 287,232 students took AP Biology. The score distribution looked like this: 18.9% earned a 5, 24.1% a 4, 27.4% a 3, 21.0% a 2, and 8.6% a 1. In 2026, the 5-rate dipped to approximately 15%, though the overall pass rate held steady at about 71%. The exam is gettable, but the shift toward application-based questions means pure memorization won’t carry you.


## FRQ Command Verbs: The Glossary Section Most Guides Skip


This is where students lose the most points, and it has nothing to do with biology knowledge. Chief Reader Reports from 2023 through 2025 consistently identify the same problem: students answer the wrong verb. They describe when the question asks them to justify. They state a prediction without explaining the reasoning behind it.


Practitioners on Reddit confirm this. In r/APStudents threads, students who scored 5s frequently mention that understanding what each question word demands was the turning point in their prep.


Here are the command verbs you need to know as precisely as any biology term:


**Describe** — State what is happening. Observations, characteristics, or steps in a process. No “why” needed.


**Explain** — Go beyond what is happening and state why or how it happens. Requires a mechanism or reasoning.


**Identify** — Name or point to something specific. Brief and direct, no elaboration required.


**Justify** — Provide evidence or reasoning that supports a claim. You need both the claim and the support.


**Predict** — State what you expect will happen based on information given. The single most cited FRQ error is stating a prediction without justifying both sides. If a question says “predict and justify,” you must explain the reasoning, not just the expected outcome.


**Calculate** — Use math. Show your work. Include units.


**Design** — Outline an experimental procedure, including variables, controls, and how data will be collected.


**Evaluate** — Assess strengths, weaknesses, or validity. Requires a judgment supported by evidence.


**Construct** — Build a graph, diagram, or model. Label axes, include titles, plot data accurately.


**Compare** — Identify similarities and differences. Address both sides, not just one.


One more common mistake worth noting: writing more does not score more points. Making a correct statement and then adding a contradicting sentence afterward can cost you the point entirely. Graders look for accuracy and precision, not volume.


## Unit 1: Chemistry of Life (8–11%)


This unit builds the molecular foundation for everything else. The terms here reappear constantly in later units, so learning them well pays off all year.


**Hydrogen bond** — A weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom and a slightly negative atom (usually oxygen or nitrogen). Critical for water’s properties and DNA structure.


**Covalent bond** — A bond formed by sharing electron pairs between atoms. The backbone of organic molecules.


**Ionic bond** — A bond formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, creating oppositely charged ions that attract.


**Monomer** — A single small molecule that can bond with others to form a polymer. Amino acids, monosaccharides, and nucleotides are all monomers.


**Polymer** — A large molecule built from repeating monomer subunits. Proteins, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids are polymers.


**Dehydration synthesis** — A reaction that links monomers by removing a water molecule. Builds polymers.


**Hydrolysis** — A reaction that breaks polymers into monomers by adding water. The reverse of dehydration synthesis.


**Carbohydrate** — An organic molecule made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Functions include energy storage (starch, glycogen) and structural support (cellulose, chitin).


**Lipid** — A hydrophobic organic molecule. Includes fats, phospholipids, and steroids. Key for energy storage and membrane structure.


**Protein** — A polymer of amino acids folded into a specific 3D shape. Functions include enzymes, structural support, transport, and signaling.


**Nucleic acid** — DNA or RNA. Polymers of nucleotides that store and transmit genetic information.


**Amino acid** — The monomer of proteins. Twenty different amino acids, each with a unique R-group (side chain) that determines its properties.


**Peptide bond** — The covalent bond linking amino acids in a protein chain. Formed by dehydration synthesis.


**Enzyme** — A biological catalyst (usually a protein) that speeds up chemical reactions by lowering activation energy.


**Active site** — The specific region on an enzyme where the substrate binds. Shape determines function.


**Substrate** — The molecule an enzyme acts on. Fits into the active site.


**pH** — A measure of hydrogen ion concentration. The scale runs from 0 (most acidic) to 14 (most basic), with 7 being neutral.


**Buffer** — A substance that resists changes in pH. Bicarbonate in blood is a classic example.


**FRQ watch:** Expect questions asking you to explain how changes in pH or temperature affect enzyme activity. The connection between protein shape (tertiary structure) and function shows up repeatedly.


## Unit 2: Cell Structure and Function (10–13%)


This unit covers cell types, organelles, and membrane transport. The membrane transport terms are especially important for FRQs because they connect to cellular energetics and homeostasis.


**Prokaryotic cell** — A cell lacking a membrane-bound nucleus (bacteria, archaea). Has ribosomes and a plasma membrane but no organelles like mitochondria.


**Eukaryotic cell** — A cell with a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles. Plants, animals, fungi, and protists are eukaryotes.


**Mitochondria** — The organelle where cellular respiration occurs. Has a double membrane; the inner membrane is where the electron transport chain runs.


**Chloroplast** — The organelle where photosynthesis occurs in plant and algal cells. Contains thylakoids (light reactions) and stroma (Calvin cycle).


**Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)** — A membrane network connected to the nucleus. Rough ER has ribosomes and makes proteins; smooth ER synthesizes lipids and detoxifies substances.


**Golgi apparatus** — Modifies, packages, and ships proteins and lipids received from the ER.


**Ribosome** — The molecular machine that translates mRNA into protein. Found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.


**Nucleus** — The membrane-bound organelle housing DNA in eukaryotic cells. Site of DNA replication and transcription.


**Phospholipid bilayer** — Two layers of phospholipids forming the core of cell membranes. Hydrophilic heads face outward, hydrophobic tails face inward.


**Fluid mosaic model** — The accepted model of membrane structure: a fluid bilayer with proteins, cholesterol, and carbohydrates embedded or attached.


**Selective permeability** — The membrane’s ability to allow some substances through while blocking others. Small nonpolar molecules pass easily; ions and large polar molecules cannot.


**Osmosis** — The diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, from areas of lower solute concentration to higher.


**Diffusion** — The net movement of molecules from high to low concentration. No energy required.


**Facilitated diffusion** — Diffusion through membrane proteins (channels or carriers). Still passive, still down the concentration gradient.


**Active transport** — Movement of molecules against the concentration gradient. Requires ATP.


**Endocytosis** — The cell engulfs material by folding the membrane inward. Includes phagocytosis and pinocytosis.


**Exocytosis** — The cell releases material by fusing vesicles with the plasma membrane.


**Tonicity** — The relative solute concentration of a solution compared to the cell. Hypertonic (more solute outside), hypotonic (less solute outside), isotonic (equal).


**Water potential** — A measure of the tendency of water to move from one area to another. Equals pressure potential plus solute potential. This is one of the most commonly confused concepts on the exam, as students mix up sign conventions and the relationship between solute potential and osmotic potential.


**FRQ watch:** Water potential calculations appear regularly. Know the formula (Ψ = Ψp + Ψs), understand that solute potential is always negative or zero, and practice interpreting which direction water flows.


## Unit 3: Cellular Energetics (12–16%) ⭐ High Weight


This unit covers photosynthesis and cellular respiration, two of the most complex and most tested processes in AP Biology. If you’re building an AP biology study guide for yourself, spend extra time here.


**ATP (adenosine triphosphate)** — The primary energy currency of cells. Energy is released when the terminal phosphate group is removed (hydrolysis). A common exam mistake: students describe ATP hydrolysis as breaking hydrogen bonds or phosphodiester bonds. The correct answer requires recognizing that a covalent phosphoanhydride bond is broken.


**ADP (adenosine diphosphate)** — The molecule left after ATP loses a phosphate group. Recycled back to ATP by adding a phosphate via cellular respiration or photosynthesis.


**Activation energy** — The minimum energy needed to start a chemical reaction. Enzymes lower this barrier.


**Photosynthesis** — The process that converts light energy, water, and CO₂ into glucose and oxygen. Occurs in chloroplasts.


**Light-dependent reactions** — The first stage of photosynthesis, occurring in the thylakoid membranes. Water is split, oxygen is released, and ATP and NADPH are produced.


**Calvin cycle** — The second stage of photosynthesis, occurring in the stroma. Uses ATP and NADPH from light reactions to fix CO₂ into G3P (a sugar precursor).


**Cellular respiration** — The process that breaks down glucose to produce ATP. Occurs in the cytoplasm (glycolysis) and mitochondria (Krebs cycle, ETC).


**Glycolysis** — The first step of cellular respiration. Splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm. Produces a small net gain of ATP and NADH.


**Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle)** — Occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. Oxidizes acetyl-CoA, producing CO₂, NADH, FADH₂, and a small amount of ATP.


**Electron transport chain (ETC)** — A series of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane (or thylakoid membrane in photosynthesis). Electrons pass down the chain, releasing energy used to pump H⁺ ions and drive ATP synthesis.


**Oxidative phosphorylation** — The production of ATP using energy from the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis. Produces the majority of ATP during cellular respiration.


**Chemiosmosis** — The flow of H⁺ ions down their concentration gradient through ATP synthase, driving ATP production. Occurs in both mitochondria and chloroplasts.


**Fermentation** — An anaerobic pathway that regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen. Produces either ethanol (yeast) or lactate (muscle cells).


**NADH / FADH₂** — Electron carriers that shuttle high-energy electrons to the ETC. NADH delivers electrons at Complex I, FADH₂ at Complex II.


**Chlorophyll** — The primary pigment in photosynthesis. Absorbs red and blue light, reflects green.


**Thylakoid** — A membrane-bound compartment inside chloroplasts where light-dependent reactions occur.


**Stroma** — The fluid-filled space inside the chloroplast, outside the thylakoids. Site of the Calvin cycle.


**FRQ watch:** Comparing photosynthesis and cellular respiration (inputs, outputs, locations, energy carriers) is one of the most frequent FRQ topics. Know which process occurs where, and be able to trace the flow of energy and matter through both.


If you want to test your understanding of these high-weight concepts, working through[practice questions](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-questions) can reveal gaps you didn’t know you had.


## Unit 4: Cell Communication and Cell Cycle (10–15%)


**Signal transduction** — The process by which a cell converts an extracellular signal into an intracellular response. Three stages: reception, transduction, response.


**Receptor** — A protein that binds a specific signaling molecule (ligand) and initiates a cellular response. Can be on the cell surface or inside the cell.


**Ligand** — A molecule that binds to a receptor. Hormones, neurotransmitters, and growth factors are common ligands.


**Second messenger** — A small intracellular molecule (like cAMP or calcium ions) that relays and amplifies signals from receptors to target molecules inside the cell.


**Kinase cascade** — A series of protein kinases that activate each other in sequence, amplifying the original signal. Each activated enzyme acts on many copies of the next, which is why amplification occurs. Chief Reader Reports note that most students invoke “amplification” as a label without explaining this mechanism, and lose points for it.


**Apoptosis** — Programmed cell death. A controlled process that eliminates damaged or unnecessary cells without triggering inflammation.


**Cell cycle** — The ordered sequence of events in which a cell grows, replicates its DNA, and divides. Includes interphase and the mitotic phase.


**Interphase** — The longest phase of the cell cycle. Includes G1 (growth), S (DNA synthesis), and G2 (preparation for mitosis).


**Mitosis** — Division of the nucleus into two genetically identical daughter nuclei. Includes prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase.


**Cytokinesis** — Division of the cytoplasm following mitosis. In animal cells, a cleavage furrow pinches inward; in plant cells, a cell plate forms.


**Cyclin / CDK (cyclin-dependent kinase)** — Regulatory proteins that control progression through the cell cycle. Cyclin levels rise and fall; CDKs are only active when bound to cyclins.


**Tumor suppressor gene** — A gene whose protein product inhibits cell division (e.g., p53, Rb). Mutations that inactivate tumor suppressors can lead to uncontrolled growth.


**Oncogene** — A mutated proto-oncogene that promotes excessive cell division. Gain-of-function mutations can contribute to cancer.


**Positive feedback** — A response that amplifies the original stimulus. Example: oxytocin during childbirth.


**Negative feedback** — A response that reduces the original stimulus, maintaining homeostasis. Example: thermoregulation.


**FRQ watch:** Signal transduction questions frequently ask you to explain how amplification occurs at each step. Don’t just say “the signal gets amplified.” Describe the mechanism: one enzyme activates many copies of its substrate protein.


## Unit 5: Heredity (8–11%)


Despite its relatively low exam weight, this unit is conceptually dense. The math-based genetics problems can eat up time if you haven’t practiced them.


**Meiosis** — A type of cell division that produces four genetically unique haploid cells (gametes) from one diploid cell. Two rounds of division.


**Crossing over** — The exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes during meiosis I. Increases genetic variation.


**Independent assortment** — Homologous chromosomes orient randomly during meiosis I, producing different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in gametes.


**Segregation** — Mendel’s law stating that allele pairs separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele for each gene.


**Allele** — An alternative form of a gene. Different alleles produce variations in traits.


**Genotype** — The genetic makeup of an organism (e.g., Bb). Determines the range of possible phenotypes.


**Phenotype** — The observable characteristics of an organism (e.g., brown eyes). Influenced by genotype and environment.


**Homozygous** — Having two identical alleles for a gene (BB or bb).


**Heterozygous** — Having two different alleles for a gene (Bb).


**Dominant** — An allele that is expressed in the phenotype when at least one copy is present.


**Recessive** — An allele that is only expressed when two copies are present (homozygous recessive).


**Punnett square** — A diagram used to predict the genotype and phenotype ratios of offspring from a genetic cross.


**Sex-linked trait** — A trait controlled by a gene on the X chromosome. Males (XY) are more likely to express recessive X-linked traits because they have only one X.


**Polygenic inheritance** — A trait controlled by multiple genes (e.g., height, skin color). Produces a continuous range of phenotypes.


**Epistasis** — When one gene’s expression masks or modifies the expression of another gene.


**Non-disjunction** — The failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis. Produces gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers (e.g., Down syndrome from trisomy 21).


**Incomplete dominance** — A blending pattern where the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype (e.g., red × white = pink).


**Codominance** — Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (e.g., AB blood type).


**FRQ watch:** Chi-square analysis questions appear in this unit. Know when to use it (testing whether observed ratios differ significantly from expected ratios), what the null hypothesis is (no significant difference), and how to interpret the p-value.


## Unit 6: Gene Expression and Regulation (12–16%) ⭐ High Weight


This unit connects DNA to the proteins that run the cell. It also includes the biotechnology topics that show up in design-an-experiment FRQs.


**DNA replication** — The process of copying DNA before cell division. Semi-conservative: each new molecule has one original strand and one new strand.


**Transcription** — Copying a gene’s DNA sequence into mRNA. Occurs in the nucleus. RNA polymerase reads the template strand and builds a complementary mRNA.


**Translation** — Building a protein from the mRNA sequence. Occurs at ribosomes. tRNA molecules deliver amino acids matching each codon.


**mRNA (messenger RNA)** — Carries the genetic code from DNA in the nucleus to ribosomes in the cytoplasm.


**tRNA (transfer RNA)** — Brings specific amino acids to the ribosome during translation. Has an anticodon that base-pairs with the mRNA codon.


**rRNA (ribosomal RNA)** — A structural and catalytic component of ribosomes.


**Codon** — A sequence of three mRNA nucleotides that codes for a specific amino acid (or a stop signal).


**Anticodon** — A three-nucleotide sequence on tRNA that is complementary to a specific mRNA codon.


**Promoter** — A DNA sequence where RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription. Determines which strand is read and in which direction.


**Gene regulation** — The mechanisms that control when, where, and how much a gene is expressed. Occurs at multiple levels (transcriptional, post-transcriptional, translational, post-translational).


**Operon** — A cluster of genes under the control of a single promoter (found in prokaryotes). The lac operon is inducible (turns on when lactose is present); the trp operon is repressible (turns off when tryptophan is abundant).


**Epigenetics** — Heritable changes in gene expression that don’t involve changes to the DNA sequence. Includes DNA methylation and histone modification.


**Mutation** — A permanent change in the DNA sequence. Can be beneficial, neutral, or harmful.


**Point mutation** — A change in a single nucleotide. Includes silent, missense, and nonsense mutations.


**Frameshift mutation** — An insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame, typically altering every amino acid downstream.


**Gel electrophoresis** — A technique that separates DNA, RNA, or protein fragments by size using an electric field. Smaller fragments move farther.


**PCR (polymerase chain reaction)** — A technique that amplifies a specific DNA segment, producing millions of copies from a small sample.


**CRISPR** — A gene-editing tool that uses a guide RNA to direct the Cas9 enzyme to cut DNA at a specific location. Allows precise insertion, deletion, or modification of genes.


**FRQ watch:** Expect questions asking you to design an experiment using gel electrophoresis or PCR. You’ll need to describe the procedure, identify controls, and predict results. CRISPR questions are increasingly common and may ask you to evaluate ethical implications.


## Unit 7: Natural Selection (13–20%) ⭐ Highest Weight


At 13–20% of the exam, this is the unit you absolutely cannot afford to underprep. Evolution is the unifying theme of biology, and College Board treats it accordingly.


**Natural selection** — The process by which organisms with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more than others. Requires variation, heritability, and differential reproduction.


**Fitness** — An organism’s reproductive success relative to others in the population. Not about strength; it’s about passing on alleles.


**Adaptation** — A heritable trait that increases an organism’s fitness in a particular environment.


**Speciation** — The formation of new species. Allopatric speciation involves geographic isolation; sympatric speciation occurs without physical separation (often through polyploidy in plants).


**Genetic drift** — Random changes in allele frequencies, most significant in small populations. Not driven by selection.


**Gene flow** — The transfer of alleles between populations through migration. Tends to reduce genetic differences between populations.


**Founder effect** — A form of genetic drift that occurs when a small group establishes a new population, carrying only a subset of the original population’s alleles.


**Bottleneck effect** — A drastic reduction in population size (from a disaster, for example) that reduces genetic variation.


**Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium** — A theoretical model in which allele frequencies remain constant across generations. Requires five conditions: large population, no mutation, no migration, random mating, and no selection. Real populations never meet all five, which is the point. The model serves as a null hypothesis for detecting evolutionary change. Students commonly memorize the five conditions but struggle to apply deviations to predict how allele frequencies shift.


**Directional selection** — Favors one extreme phenotype, shifting the population’s trait distribution in one direction.


**Stabilizing selection** — Favors the intermediate phenotype, reducing variation.


**Disruptive selection** — Favors both extreme phenotypes over the intermediate, potentially splitting a population.


**Phylogeny** — The evolutionary history and relationships among organisms or groups.


**Cladogram** — A branching diagram showing evolutionary relationships based on shared derived characteristics.


**Homologous structures** — Structures in different species that share a common evolutionary origin but may have different functions (e.g., bat wing and human arm).


**Analogous structures** — Structures in different species that have similar functions but different evolutionary origins (e.g., bat wing and insect wing). Result of convergent evolution.


**Convergent evolution** — Unrelated species independently evolve similar traits due to similar environmental pressures.


**Divergent evolution** — Related species evolve different traits as they adapt to different environments.


**Coevolution** — Two species evolve in response to each other (e.g., predator-prey arms races, pollinator-flower relationships).


**Endosymbiotic theory** — The theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts originated as free-living prokaryotes engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells. Supported by their double membranes, own DNA, and ribosome similarity to bacteria.


**FRQ watch:** Hardy-Weinberg calculations are a near-certainty. Practice both the allele frequency equations (p + q = 1) and the genotype frequency equations (p² + 2pq + q² = 1). Be prepared to explain which condition is violated in a given scenario and what that means for the population’s evolution.


## Unit 8: Ecology (10–15%)


**Population** — A group of individuals of the same species living in the same area at the same time.


**Community** — All the populations of different species living and interacting in a given area.


**Ecosystem** — A community of organisms plus the abiotic (nonliving) factors in their environment.


**Biome** — A large geographic region characterized by specific climate conditions and dominant plant types (e.g., tropical rainforest, tundra, desert).


**Food web** — A model showing the complex feeding relationships within a community. More realistic than a simple food chain.


**Trophic level** — A feeding position in a food web. Producers are the first level, followed by primary consumers, secondary consumers, and so on.


**Energy pyramid** — A diagram showing that energy decreases at each trophic level. Only about 10% of energy transfers from one level to the next.


**Primary productivity** — The rate at which producers (plants, algae) convert light energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis.


**Carrying capacity (K)** — The maximum population size an environment can sustain indefinitely given available resources.


**Logistic growth** — Population growth that slows as the population approaches carrying capacity. Produces an S-shaped curve.


**Exponential growth** — Unrestricted population growth producing a J-shaped curve. Occurs when resources are unlimited (rare in nature for sustained periods).


**Density-dependent factors** — Factors whose effects intensify as population density increases (e.g., competition, disease, predation).


**Density-independent factors** — Factors that affect populations regardless of density (e.g., natural disasters, climate events).


**Symbiosis** — A close ecological relationship between two species. Mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected), parasitism (one benefits, the other is harmed).


**Keystone species** — A species whose impact on its community is disproportionately large relative to its abundance. Removal causes major ecosystem changes.


**Biogeochemical cycle** — The recycling of matter (carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, water) through living and nonliving components of an ecosystem.


**Succession** — The gradual change in species composition over time. Primary succession begins on bare rock or new land; secondary succession follows a disturbance in an area with existing soil.


**FRQ watch:** Ecology FRQs often ask you to interpret data from field studies or calculate growth rates. Know how to read and construct graphs of population growth, and be prepared to explain why populations fluctuate.


## The Six Science Practices


AP Biology doesn’t just test what you know. It tests what you can do with what you know. The College Board explicitly scores six science practices on both the MCQ and FRQ sections. Understanding them changes how you study.


**Practice 1: Concept Explanation** — Can you explain biological concepts and processes? This is the most straightforward practice, but “explain” requires mechanism, not just labels.


**Practice 2: Visual Representations** — Can you analyze and create models, diagrams, and other visual representations of biological concepts? Think: interpreting a diagram of the cell membrane, drawing a cladogram, or reading a signal transduction pathway.


**Practice 3: Questions and Methods** — Can you determine scientific questions and methods? This is the experimental design practice. It shows up in “Design an experiment” FRQs.


**Practice 4: Representing and Describing Data** — Can you represent data in tables, charts, and graphs, and describe patterns? Constructing a graph with proper labels and interpreting trends are both tested.


**Practice 5: Statistical Tests and Data Analysis** — Can you perform statistical analyses and evaluate experimental results? Chi-square tests, standard error bars, and identifying whether data supports or refutes a hypothesis all fall here.


**Practice 6: Argumentation** — Can you develop and justify scientific arguments? This is the highest-order practice. It requires you to make a claim, support it with evidence, and provide reasoning. The “justify” and “evaluate” FRQ verbs map directly to this practice.


The shift in recent exam cycles has been unmistakable: the content stays the same 8 units, but questions increasingly demand application, data interpretation, and argumentation over recall.


## Commonly Confused Terms


These mix-ups cost students easy points every year. Here are the pairs that trip people up most, based on Chief Reader Reports and student discussions on forums:


### Osmosis vs. Diffusion


Osmosis Diffusion


What moves Water Solute molecules


Direction Low solute → high solute (across a membrane) High concentration → low concentration


Membrane required? Yes No (but can occur across one)


### Mitosis vs. Meiosis


Mitosis Meiosis


Result 2 identical diploid cells 4 unique haploid cells


Divisions 1 2


Purpose Growth, repair Gamete production


Crossing over No Yes (meiosis I)


### DNA vs. RNA


DNA RNA


Sugar Deoxyribose Ribose


Bases A, T, G, C A, U, G, C


Strands Double Usually single


Location Nucleus (mostly) Nucleus and cytoplasm


### Photosynthesis vs. Cellular Respiration


Photosynthesis Cellular Respiration


Inputs CO₂ + H₂O + light Glucose + O₂


Outputs Glucose + O₂ CO₂ + H₂O + ATP


Where Chloroplasts Cytoplasm + Mitochondria


Energy Light → chemical (glucose) Chemical (glucose) → ATP


### Genotype vs. Phenotype


Genotype Phenotype


Definition The alleles an organism has The observable trait expressed


Example Bb Brown eyes


Determined by Inheritance Genotype + environment


### Homologous vs. Analogous Structures


Homologous Analogous


Origin Common ancestor Different ancestors


Function May differ Similar


Evidence for Divergent evolution Convergent evolution


## How to Use This AP Biology Study Guide in Your Study Plan


A glossary is useful only if you actively engage with it. Here’s how to make this reference work for you rather than just sit in a browser tab.


**Step 1: Prioritize by weight.** Start with Units 3, 6, and 7. Together they can represent over half your exam score. Don’t give every unit equal study time.


**Step 2: Test yourself.** After reading through a unit’s terms, close this page and write down every term you can remember with its definition. The ones you miss are your study targets.


**Step 3: Practice with FRQ verbs.** Pick a term and try to answer it using different command verbs. For example, take “chemiosmosis” and practice describing it, explaining why it produces ATP, and predicting what happens if the H⁺ gradient is disrupted. This trains you for the exam’s actual question format.


**Step 4: Use the confusion-buster tables.** Before your exam, review the commonly confused terms. These are free points you can protect.


**Step 5: Take full practice exams.** Vocabulary knowledge needs to translate into timed performance. Full-length[practice tests](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-tests) simulate test-day pressure and reveal whether you can apply terms under time constraints.


For students prepping for multiple standardized tests alongside AP exams, building a[personalized study plan](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/study-plan-generator) can help you allocate time across all your commitments without burning out.


If you’re looking for broader AP exam prep strategies beyond biology, our guide to the[best AP study resources](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/best-ap-study-resources) covers tools and approaches across multiple subjects.


The bottom line: AP Biology rewards students who understand terms deeply enough to use them, not just recognize them. This AP biology study guide gives you the terms. The exam will ask you to apply them. Bridge that gap with practice, and a 4 or 5 is well within reach.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How many units are on the AP Biology exam?


There are 8 units: Chemistry of Life, Cell Structure and Function, Cellular Energetics, Cell Communication and Cell Cycle, Heredity, Gene Expression and Regulation, Natural Selection, and Ecology. They range from 8% to 20% of the exam weight.


### Which AP Biology units should I study first?


Start with Units 3 (Cellular Energetics), 6 (Gene Expression), and 7 (Natural Selection). Combined, they account for 37–52% of the exam. Unit 7 carries the single highest weight at 13–20%.


### What is the pass rate for AP Biology?


About 70–71% of students score a 3 or higher. In 2025, 287,232 students took the exam, and 18.9% earned a 5. The 5-rate dipped to approximately 15% in 2026, though the overall pass rate remained stable.


### What are FRQ command verbs, and why do they matter?


Command verbs like “describe,” “explain,” “justify,” and “predict” tell you exactly what the exam expects in your response. Answering to the wrong verb (for example, describing when the question asked you to justify) is one of the most common and most avoidable ways to lose points, according to College Board Chief Reader Reports.


### How long is the AP Biology exam?


The exam is 3 hours total. Section I gives you 90 minutes for 60 multiple-choice questions. Section II gives you 90 minutes for 6 free-response questions (2 long, 4 short).


### Is the AP Biology exam going digital?


Starting in 2026, AP Biology uses a hybrid digital format. You answer multiple-choice questions and view FRQ prompts in Bluebook (the College Board’s digital testing app), then handwrite your free-response answers in a paper booklet.


### What is the most common mistake on AP Biology FRQs?


The single most cited error across recent exam cycles is stating a prediction without justifying both sides. Students write what they expect will happen but stop there, failing to provide the reasoning that earns the full points. Writing too much is also risky, because a contradicting statement after a correct answer can cost you the point.


### How should I use a glossary to study for AP Biology?


Don’t just read through it passively. Use active recall: cover the definitions and try to explain each term from memory. Practice answering terms using different FRQ command verbs. Focus your time on the highest-weight units, and use the commonly confused terms section to protect against careless errors on exam day.
